EVENT RENTAL INVENTORY PAYBACK CALCULATOR · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER · NOTHING UPLOADED

Which rental items pay for themselves? Payback, return and what to buy next

For party, tent and event rental companies. List the chairs, tables, linens and floors you own or plan to buy. The tool counts handling per rental, card fees, breakage and loss, storage and each item's wear, then ranks every item by return on the money tied up, shows payback and break-even rentals per unit, and finds the lowest rental price that pays an item back in the years you choose.

The method with a worked example: which rental items pay for themselves.

1. Your rules

2. Your items

One row per kind of item. Rentals per unit per year is how many events each unit goes out to. Handling is the washing, pressing, loading and counting cost for one unit on one rental. Loss and damage is the share of units broken or missing in a year.

ItemUnits ownedCost per unit ($)Price per unit per rental ($)Rentals per unit per yearHandling per rental ($)Loss and damage (% of units a year)Storage per unit per year ($)Useful life (years)

Fill in the rows, then click Rank my inventory.

Result

RankItemInvestedCash a yearReturnPayback (years)Break-even rentals per unitLowest price for your paybackProfit a year after wear

Returns assume extra units rent as often as the ones you own. If you already turn away orders for an item the return on more of it is real; if the stock sits idle on busy weekends it is not.

How it is built

Cash a year for an item is units × rentals × price, minus handling on every rental, card fees on the revenue, the units lost or broken each year at replacement cost, and storage. Payback is what the units cost divided by that cash. Profit after wear also takes off cost ÷ useful life. Break-even rentals is the number of rentals per unit where that profit is zero.

Lowest price: the price at which cash a year equals cost ÷ the payback you want. The test suite checks that renting at exactly that price pays back in exactly that time for hundreds of random items.

Common questions

Which rental item should I buy next?

Rank every item by what a year of rentals returns on the money tied up in it: rentals times price, minus handling, card fees, losses and storage, divided by what the units cost. The item at the top returns the most on each dollar. This assumes the extra units rent as often as the ones you own, so check how often you are already sold out before you add stock.

How do I know if a rental item has paid for itself?

Divide what the units cost by the cash they bring in a year after handling, card fees, breakage and storage. That is the payback in years. Compare it with the useful life: an item that pays back in three years but wears out in three has returned nothing.

What should I charge to rent an item so it pays back in two years?

Work backwards: the yearly share of the purchase cost needed for the payback you want, plus storage and expected losses, spread over the rentals each unit gets, plus the handling cost of each rental, divided by one minus your card fee. The calculator shows that lowest price for every item.

How many times a year does a rental item have to go out to break even?

Add the item's yearly wear (cost divided by useful life), storage and expected losses per unit, then divide by what one rental earns after handling and card fees. Below that number of rentals per unit the item loses money even if it is always in use for a customer.

Is my data uploaded?

No. Everything runs in your browser, there are no accounts, and nothing is sent to a server. Use Save to download a scenario file.

Is this tax, insurance or business advice?

No. It is arithmetic on the numbers you type. Depreciation for tax, sales tax on rentals and insurance depend on where you operate. Check with an accountant or your insurer.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is arithmetic on the numbers you type, not tax, legal, insurance or financial advice. Use at your own risk. Check taxes, insurance and your contracts with an accountant or adviser.

Independent. Not affiliated with any rental software, equipment maker or industry association, and none is named or ranked here.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime or backups of anything you enter.

Everything runs in your browser. Your numbers are never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors. Anonymous feature events (inventory_ranked, example_loaded, text_copied, csv_downloaded, file_saved) are counted in this browser only, and you can switch that off below.

Related tool: the tent rental job profit calculator, for the profit on a single job.

Which rental items pay for themselves?

Chairs and dance floors both look busy on a Saturday. Per dollar tied up, one of them returns almost six times what the other does.

The worked example

A rental company owns 150 Chiavari chairs at $48 each, $7,200 in total. Each chair goes out 14 times a year at $6.50 a rental, so the chairs bring in $13,650. Washing and loading costs $0.60 a chair a rental ($1,260 a year), card fees at 3% take $410, 2% of the chairs break or go missing ($144 to replace) and storage is $1.10 a chair ($165).

LinePer year
Cash after handling, fees, losses and storage$11,672
Wear (cost over 8 years)$900
Profit after wear$10,772
Return on the money tied up162.1%
Payback0.6 years

Each chair has to go out 1.4 times a year before it covers its wear, storage and losses. It goes out 14 times.

The item that looks as busy but is not as good

The dance floor panels cost $210 each and rent for $14, but they go out only 6 times a year and cost $8 a panel to store. They return 28.3% a year against 162.1% for the chairs and take 3.5 years to pay back.

To pay back in two years the panels would have to rent for $21.84, which is $7.84 more than $14.00. Folding chairs, by comparison, return 160.4% and pay back in 0.6 years at $1.50 a rental.
